titleStmt.title: Tonotopic organization of human auditory cortex
titleStmt.author: Humphries
Liebenthal
Binder

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Tonotopic organization of human auditory cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the spatial arrangement of frequency-selective responses in human auditory cortex
span.quote: The organization of tonotopic fields in human auditory cortex was investigated using functional magnetic resonance imaging.

span.label: how many tonotopic gradients human auditory cortex contains, how they are oriented relative to HG, and how far they vary across subjects
span.quote: In particular, we were interested in addressing several open questions that have not been completely resolved, such as the number of frequency gradients, the orientation of the gradients relative to HG, and the variability of the gradients across subjects.

span.label: two mirror-symmetric gradients running perpendicular to HG rather than along it, a third smaller gradient on lateral posterior STG, and a methodological diagnosis of why the previous literature disagreed
span.quote: The orientation of these two principal gradients is thus roughly perpendicular to HG, rather than parallel as previously assumed.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Two mirror-symmetric frequency gradients were found extending along an anterior-posterior axis from a zone on the lateral aspect of Heschl's gyrus (HG), which responds preferentially to lower frequencies, toward zones posterior and anterior to HG that are sensitive to higher frequencies.

span.label: tonotopic organization of human auditory cortex
span.quote: The organization of tonotopic fields in human auditory cortex was investigated using functional magnetic resonance imaging.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: FMRI data were collected from 8 right-handed subjects (7 male, 1 female; ages 20-37 years).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: cortical folding pushes the anterior and posterior high-frequency zones close together in 3-D, so volume-based smoothing and inter-subject variation blur them into one, hiding the perpendicular gradients from earlier studies
span.quote: The cortical folding that produces HG causes the high-frequency zones in the sulci posterior and anterior to HG to be physically very close in 3-dimensional space. This physical proximity, together with inter-subject variation in the exact location of the sulci and spatial smoothing used for generating group maps, may have caused these distinct high-frequency areas to blur together.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: flattening the superior temporal plane onto a surface model pulls the buried sulcal regions apart, which is what makes the perpendicular topology visible
span.quote: Flattening the superior temporal plane with surface modeling separates these regions and allows a more accurate analysis of topological relations running perpendicular to the gyrus.

span.label: cortical folding puts the anterior and posterior high-frequency zones physically close together, so volume-based analysis and smoothing blur them into one
span.quote: The cortical folding that produces HG causes the high-frequency zones in the sulci posterior and anterior to HG to be physically very close in 3-dimensional space. This physical proximity, together with inter-subject variation in the exact location of the sulci and spatial smoothing used for generating group maps, may have caused these distinct high-frequency areas to blur together.

span.label: flattening the superior temporal plane separates regions that are adjacent in 3-D, making gradients perpendicular to the gyrus visible
span.quote: Flattening the superior temporal plane with surface modeling separates these regions and allows a more accurate analysis of topological relations running perpendicular to the gyrus.

span.label: sparse sampling: the scanner runs only in a 1.6 s silent gap after the 8 s tone sequence, so scanner noise never overlaps the stimulus
span.quote: A trial lasted 9.6 seconds and started with an 8-second tone sequence followed by a 1.6-second gap. MRI scanning was performed only during the 1.6-second gap to prevent interference from scanner noise during presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: stochastic alternation between two- and three-tone bursts holds the cortical response up, since auditory neurons adapt after onset
span.quote: This alternating pattern was designed to provoke large responses in auditory cortical neurons, which tend to have increased firing rates at stimulus onset but often return to baseline before the end of the stimulus

span.label: tone ratios chosen so the composite produces no harmonic relationship and no missing-fundamental pitch
span.quote: These ratios were selected so that the composite tones would have no harmonic relationships and would not produce a “missing fundamental” pitch, and so that the five tones comprising the stimulus train would be approximately equidistant in pitch space.

span.label: best frequency is interpolated between the six tested bands by weighting adjacent conditions, giving finer resolution than the design has
span.quote: Intermediate frequencies of best response at each point on the surface were determined by first selecting a subset of the frequencies that showed greater activation than the mean at that point. For the majority of surface points this consisted of one, two, or three adjacent frequencies. The activation levels for this set of frequencies were normalized to produce a weight vector, which was then multiplied by the corresponding log-transformed frequencies and summed. The resulting number was mapped to a log-scaled color map.

span.label: landmark-based surface alignment rather than volumetric alignment, for spatial precision in the temporal lobe
span.quote: Landmark-based alignment has been shown to increase spatial precision along the cortical surface of the temporal lobe in comparison to volumetric alignment

span.label: non-parametric permutation testing because eight subjects will not support a parametric group test
span.quote: Because of the small number of subjects, significance was calculated using a non-parametric permutation test

span.label: several sessions per subject, to buy single-subject statistical power and a test-retest estimate at the same time
span.quote: Multiple sessions were used to increase the total number of trials in order to gain statistical power for single subject analyses, and to enable a qualitative assessment of the test-retest variability of tonotopic responses.

span.label: The core/belt boundary drawn on the homology map cannot be established from frequency responses alone and is an estimate imported from macaque anatomy and human cytoarchitecture.
span.quote: The exact boundary between core and belt cannot be determined based solely on frequency response, thus this line is an estimate guided by the known topographical organization in the macaque and by previous human cytoarchitectonic studies ( Fullerton and Pandya 2007 ; Morosan et al., 2001 ; Rivier and Clarke 1997 ).

span.label: The absence of a gradient corresponding to macaque area RT may be a sensitivity failure of the stimuli rather than evidence that the area is absent in humans.
span.quote: The lack of frequency-selective activation in this region could be due to low sensitivity to the stimuli used in the current study.

span.label: The sample was small enough to force non-parametric permutation testing for the group analysis.
span.quote: Because of the small number of subjects, significance was calculated using a non-parametric permutation test ( Nichols and Holmes 2002 ).

span.label: the tested range truncates the tuning estimate, so points preferring 200 or 6400 Hz were excluded from that analysis
span.quote: Points were also excluded if their largest response was to the lowest (200 Hz) or highest (6400 Hz) frequency. The reason for this is that activation levels at the lowest and highest frequencies may not reflect the largest possible response for that brain area, because the area could possibly have larger responses to even lower or higher frequencies that were not included in the experiment. Therefore, normalized values for these regions could be inaccurate.

span.label: an absence the authors decline to resolve: no anterior RT-like gradient, which may be the stimuli or may be the species
span.quote: The lack of frequency-selective activation in this region could be due to low sensitivity to the stimuli used in the current study. Alternatively, it is possible that area RT does not exist in humans.

span.label: the sharper-tuning reading is undercut by the authors themselves, because the effect tracks overall response strength
span.quote: We note, however, that these patterns generally appear to be correlated with the overall strength of the response. That is, increased differences in the response to the preferred versus non-preferred frequencies are driven primarily by increases in response to the preferred frequency rather than decreases in the response to the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: the core/belt boundary cannot be fixed from frequency response alone, so the line drawn is an estimate imported from other evidence
span.quote: The exact boundary between core and belt cannot be determined based solely on frequency response, thus this line is an estimate guided by the known topographical organization in the macaque and by previous human cytoarchitectonic studies

span.label: apparent parietal operculum activation is an artifact of volume-to-surface mapping, not a finding
span.quote: Inspection of the data in native volume space, however, showed that this activation is primarily an artifact of the mapping between volume and surface spaces due to partial volume effects (i.e., some voxels span both the upper and lower bank of the sulcus) and small amounts of error in the representation of the surface mesh, which can interfere with accurate separation of functional data from the closely apposed superior temporal plane and parietal operculum.

span.label: high variability across subjects and hemispheres in where the low-frequency border between gradients falls
span.quote: The maps in our study did show a high degree of variability across subjects and across hemispheres. For example, the location of the low-frequency border between the two gradients varied in relation to HG.

span.label: inter-session variability attributed partly to head movement and partly to unmeasured attention and alertness
span.quote: However, some inter-session variability was seen in the number of significantly activated voxels and their preferred frequency. Some of this variance can be attributed to differences across sessions in the amount of head movement and other artifacts. Another possible source of variance is physiologic state changes such as alterations in attention and alertness.

span.label: eight subjects, seven of them male
span.quote: FMRI data were collected from 8 right-handed subjects (7 male, 1 female; ages 20-37 years).

span.label: no task was performed, so attentional state during scanning is uncontrolled by design
span.quote: During the sessions subjects were instructed to lie still and listen to the tones. No specific task was performed during the experiment.

span.label: the core/belt field layout, used as the template against which a human fMRI map is read and labelled
span.quote: In the auditory cortex of nonhuman primates, each of the three divisions of primary “core” cortex – A1, R and RT – exhibit tonotopic gradients that are mirror symmetric to each other

span.label: retinotopy used as the contrast case for how a receptive-field gradient behaves at an areal boundary
span.quote: In contrast to the visual cortex, where retinotopic gradients reverse direction at the boundary between primary and secondary cortices, the receptive field gradients in auditory cortex run parallel to the primary/secondary (i.e., core/belt) boundary, such that the two mirror symmetric gradients observed in A1 and R extend laterally to belt areas ML and AL

span.label: cortical folding
span.quote: The cortical folding that produces HG causes the high-frequency zones in the sulci posterior and anterior to HG to be physically very close in 3-dimensional space. This physical proximity, together with inter-subject variation in the exact location of the sulci and spatial smoothing used for generating group maps, may have caused these distinct high-frequency areas to blur together.

span.label: physical proximity
span.quote: The cortical folding that produces HG causes the high-frequency zones in the sulci posterior and anterior to HG to be physically very close in 3-dimensional space. This physical proximity, together with inter-subject variation in the exact location of the sulci and spatial smoothing used for generating group maps, may have caused these distinct high-frequency areas to blur together.

span.label: tonotopy - a gradient of preferred frequency mirroring the cochlea; explicitly a map of one stimulus dimension, not of any other response property
span.quote: This organization, referred to as tonotopy or cochleotopy, mirrors the distribution of receptors in the cochlea, with a gradient extending between neurons that preferentially respond to high frequencies and those that respond best to low frequencies.

span.label: gradient - as a field bounded by high and low bands, not as a line between two poles; the paper says this reading is itself a source of the literature's disagreement
span.quote: Many authors have conceived of these gradients as extending along a narrow line between high and low poles. A consideration of the data from non-human primate studies, however, suggests instead a topography composed of alternating high and low frequency bands, each of which extends across contiguous core and belt regions

span.label: frequency-selective - defined operationally as a significant F test across the six tested frequencies, carrying no claim about tuning shape
span.quote: Voxels were identified as having a frequency-selective response if they showed significant differences in activation across the six frequencies as determined by an F test.

span.label: tuning bandwidth - here a ratio of preferred to non-preferred BOLD amplitude, which the paper scare-quotes and then declines to read as tuning width
span.quote: We note, however, that these patterns generally appear to be correlated with the overall strength of the response. That is, increased differences in the response to the preferred versus non-preferred frequencies are driven primarily by increases in response to the preferred frequency rather than decreases in the response to the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: core and belt - cytoarchitectonic and connectional divisions, explicitly not divisions defined by the frequency map being measured
span.quote: with the boundary between core and belt defined by cytoarchitectonic and connectivity patterns rather than tonotopic gradients.

span.label: corresponds to / homologous to - used hedged throughout for human-macaque field matches, never as identity
span.quote: Based on these similarities, it is likely that the two gradients observed in the current study encompass two separate regions of cortex homologous to macaque areas A1 and R.

span.label: replicates → Formisano et al. (2003); Talavage et al. (2004); Woods et al. (2009)
span.quote: These results confirm previous evidence for at least two mirror-symmetric gradients in human auditory cortex ( Formisano et al., 2003 ; Talavage et al., 2004 ; Woods et al., 2009 ).

span.label: contradicts → Formisano et al. (2003), on the orientation of the gradients relative to HG
span.note: differs in: the ORIENTATION of the gradients relative to HG: THESE GRADIENTS ARE ORIENTED APPROXIMATELY ALONG THE AXIS OF HG, WHEREAS THE GRADIENTS WE OBSERVED WERE PERPENDICULAR TO THE LONG AXIS OF HG
span.quote: Example maps in Formisano et al. suggest that these gradients are oriented approximately along the axis of HG, whereas the gradients we observed were perpendicular to the long axis of HG.

span.label: contradicts → Woods et al. (2009), on labelling the posterior lateral gradient as parabelt
span.note: differs in: where the parabelt is and whether it is tonotopic at all: THERE IS LITTLE EVIDENCE FOR TONOTOPIC ORGANIZATION IN THE PARABELT OF MONKEYS, and RECENT HUMAN CYTOARCHITECTONIC DATA SUGGEST THAT THE PARABELT IS LOCATED MORE VENTRALLY IN THE UPPER BANK OF THE SUPERIOR TEMPORAL SULCUS
span.quote: We question this interpretation given that there is little evidence for tonotopic organization in the parabelt of monkeys, and recent human cytoarchitectonic data suggest that the parabelt is located more ventrally in the upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus ( Fullerton and Pandya 2007 ).

span.label: partially-supports → Formisano et al. 2003: two mirror-symmetric gradients, but running along the axis of HG
span.quote: The highest frequency used by Formisano et al. was 3000 Hz, whereas the current study included frequencies up to 6400 Hz, suggesting that some medial regions anterior to HG that are sensitive to higher frequencies might have been missed in the earlier study.

span.label: refines → Talavage et al. 2004: three gradients described as narrow lines between high and low poles
span.quote: Many authors have conceived of these gradients as extending along a narrow line between high and low poles. A consideration of the data from non-human primate studies, however, suggests instead a topography composed of alternating high and low frequency bands, each of which extends across contiguous core and belt regions

span.label: supports → Woods et al. 2009: one low-frequency area on HG flanked by two high-frequency areas
span.quote: The highest frequency band tested by Woods et al. was 3600 Hz, compared to 6400 Hz in the current study. Compared to the stimuli in the current study, the pure tone sequences used by Woods et al. were presented at a slower frequency (4 Hz vs. 10 Hz) and had a narrower bandwidth.

span.label: contradicts → Woods et al. 2009: the posterior lateral field is parabelt
span.note: differs in: which area the same patch of cortex IS - the two papers show A SIMILAR DIAGRAM and label it differently: AREA CL here, POSTERIOR PARABELT there, and the criterion offered is that IN THE MONKEY, THIS GRADIENT DOES NOT EXTEND INTO ADJACENT AREAS; THEREFORE, ITS BOUNDARIES ARE EASILY DETERMINED
span.quote: A key feature in orienting this map is the posterior lateral gradient, which most likely corresponds to area CL. In the monkey, this gradient does not extend into adjacent areas; therefore, its boundaries are easily determined. Woods et al. (2009) , who show a similar diagram, label this section of cortex as posterior parabelt. We question this interpretation given that there is little evidence for tonotopic organization in the parabelt of monkeys, and recent human cytoarchitectonic data suggest that the parabelt is located more ventrally in the upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus

span.label: contradicts → the early two-frequency studies: a single gradient running along the axis of HG
span.note: differs in: the analysis method, named as decisive across the whole prior literature: ONE THAT WE BELIEVE IS CRITICAL IS THAT THE STUDIES REPORTING GRADIENTS PERPENDICULAR TO HG ALL USED SURFACE-BASED RATHER THAN VOLUME-BASED ANALYSIS
span.quote: Although there are many differences in methodology between these studies, one that we believe is critical is that the studies reporting gradients perpendicular to HG all used surface-based rather than volume-based analysis.

span.label: qualifies → their own reading that these central regions are more sharply tuned
span.note: differs in: which side of the difference moves: the sharper tuning is DRIVEN PRIMARILY BY INCREASES IN RESPONSE TO THE PREFERRED FREQUENCY RATHER THAN DECREASES IN THE RESPONSE TO THE NON-PREFERRED FREQUENCIES, so the pattern IS CORRELATED WITH THE OVERALL STRENGTH OF THE RESPONSE and need not be sharper tuning
span.quote: We note, however, that these patterns generally appear to be correlated with the overall strength of the response. That is, increased differences in the response to the preferred versus non-preferred frequencies are driven primarily by increases in response to the preferred frequency rather than decreases in the response to the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: supports → macaque evidence that area CM prefers higher than average frequencies without a gradient
span.quote: In the posterior medial section of the map, which we label as area CM, there does not appear to be a distinct frequency gradient. This is in agreement with evidence from the macaque suggesting that the majority of neurons in this region respond preferentially to higher than average frequencies

span.label: tonotopy —same-as→ cochleotopy
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — given as alternate names in one clause, unhedged - a positive control for the Q-32 join key
span.quote: This organization, referred to as tonotopy or cochleotopy, mirrors the distribution of receptors in the cochlea, with a gradient extending between neurons that preferentially respond to high frequencies and those that respond best to low frequencies.

span.label: frequency-selective response —operationalised-as→ F test
span.quote: Voxels were identified as having a frequency-selective response if they showed significant differences in activation across the six frequencies as determined by an F test.

span.label: surface-based —contrasted-with→ volume-based analysis
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE ANALYSIS METHOD, AND IT IS OFFERED AS THE EXPLANATION OF THE DISAGREEMENT. 'Although there are many differences in methodology between these studies, ONE THAT WE BELIEVE IS CRITICAL is that THE STUDIES REPORTING GRADIENTS PERPENDICULAR TO HG ALL USED SURFACE-BASED RATHER THAN VOLUME-BASED ANALYSIS.' The authors name the one difference they think decides the result out of many they could have named - which is the analyst decision this project exists to make legible. Q-469. · strength of the relation: 1 — the contrast the paper says explains the whole literature's disagreement
span.quote: Although there are many differences in methodology between these studies, one that we believe is critical is that the studies reporting gradients perpendicular to HG all used surface-based rather than volume-based analysis.

span.label: cortical folding —causes→ physical proximity
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: The cortical folding that produces HG causes the high-frequency zones in the sulci posterior and anterior to HG to be physically very close in 3-dimensional space. This physical proximity, together with inter-subject variation in the exact location of the sulci and spatial smoothing used for generating group maps, may have caused these distinct high-frequency areas to blur together.

span.label: RETRACTED (A HEDGED HOMOLOGY BETWEEN SPECIES, READ AS AN IDENTITY) · two principal gradients —same-as→ macaque areas A1 and R
span.note: RETRACTED: A HEDGED HOMOLOGY BETWEEN SPECIES, READ AS AN IDENTITY. The edge is `two principal gradients --same-as--> macaque areas A1 and R`. The span: 'Based on these similarities, IT IS LIKELY THAT the two gradients observed in the current study ENCOMPASS two separate regions of cortex HOMOLOGOUS TO macaque areas A1 and R.' Three separate weakenings in one sentence: `it is likely that` is a hedge, `encompass` is containment rather than identity, and `homologous to` is a claim about shared evolutionary origin between two SPECIES - the whole point of which is that the two are not the same thing. A human gradient is not a macaque area. THE RELATION THE SENTENCE STATES IS AVAILABLE: the regions the gradients encompass stand in a homology to the macaque areas, which is a `part-of` plus a cross-species correspondence the vocabulary has no type for - compare Ben-Tov2022[0], where the same homology is asserted correctly BECAUSE the edge carries `differs_in` naming what the three hundred million years changed. — strength of the relation: 0.7 — hedged - it is likely that. the weight carries the hedge, the confidence carries my reading of the sentence
span.quote: Based on these similarities, it is likely that the two gradients observed in the current study encompass two separate regions of cortex homologous to macaque areas A1 and R.

span.label: posterior lateral gradient —same-as→ area CL
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.65 — the record marks this weak — most likely corresponds to
span.quote: A key feature in orienting this map is the posterior lateral gradient, which most likely corresponds to area CL. In the monkey, this gradient does not extend into adjacent areas; therefore, its boundaries are easily determined. Woods et al. (2009) , who show a similar diagram, label this section of cortex as posterior parabelt. We question this interpretation given that there is little evidence for tonotopic organization in the parabelt of monkeys, and recent human cytoarchitectonic data suggest that the parabelt is located more ventrally in the upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus

span.label: posterior lateral gradient —distinct-from→ posterior parabelt
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — a labelling dispute with Woods et al., settled by appeal to a different evidence type
span.quote: A key feature in orienting this map is the posterior lateral gradient, which most likely corresponds to area CL. In the monkey, this gradient does not extend into adjacent areas; therefore, its boundaries are easily determined. Woods et al. (2009) , who show a similar diagram, label this section of cortex as posterior parabelt. We question this interpretation given that there is little evidence for tonotopic organization in the parabelt of monkeys, and recent human cytoarchitectonic data suggest that the parabelt is located more ventrally in the upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus

span.label: core —distinct-from→ belt
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHAT DEFINES THE BOUNDARY. 'with THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN CORE AND BELT DEFINED BY CYTOARCHITECTONIC AND CONNECTIVITY PATTERNS RATHER THAN TONOTOPIC GRADIENTS.' The two regions are not distinguished by the property the paper measures - they are distinguished by a different property entirely, so a tonotopic result cannot confirm or refute the division it is described against. Q-469. · strength of the relation: 1 — the boundary is stipulated from cytoarchitecture and connectivity, not from the phenomenon being mapped
span.quote: with the boundary between core and belt defined by cytoarchitectonic and connectivity patterns rather than tonotopic gradients.

span.label: retinotopic gradients —contrasted-with→ receptive field gradients in auditory cortex
span.term: receptive field gradients in auditory cortex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — a structural contrast between sensory systems sharing almost no vocabulary
span.quote: In contrast to the visual cortex, where retinotopic gradients reverse direction at the boundary between primary and secondary cortices, the receptive field gradients in auditory cortex run parallel to the primary/secondary (i.e., core/belt) boundary, such that the two mirror symmetric gradients observed in A1 and R extend laterally to belt areas ML and AL

span.label: general linear model
span.quote: A general linear model was applied to each voxel time series.

span.label: F-test
span.quote: F-tests were also calculated examining differences across conditions, as well as direct contrasts between high (6400, 3200 Hz), middle (800, 1600 Hz), and low (200, 400 Hz) frequencies.

span.label: multiple comparison correction
span.quote: Statistical parametric maps were initially thresholded at p<.01 and then cluster thresholded to correct for multiple comparisons at an alpha level of .05

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A random effects group analysis examined differences in the estimated coefficients across subjects using one-way ANOVA.

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: Because of the small number of subjects, significance was calculated using a non-parametric permutation test ( Nichols and Holmes 2002

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The mean between-session correlation coefficient of the tonotopy maps is .834 (SD = 0.083).

span.label: F test across six frequency conditions
span.term: F test across six frequency conditions
span.quote: Voxels were identified as having a frequency-selective response if they showed significant differences in activation across the six frequencies as determined by an F test.

span.label: cluster thresholding
span.quote: Statistical parametric maps were initially thresholded at p<.01 and then cluster thresholded to correct for multiple comparisons at an alpha level of .05 using the AFNI program AlphaSim

span.label: non-parametric permutation test
span.quote: Because of the small number of subjects, significance was calculated using a non-parametric permutation test

span.label: between-session correlation coefficient
span.quote: The mean between-session correlation coefficient of the tonotopy maps is .834 (SD = 0.083).

span.label: Two mirror-symmetric frequency gradients run anterior-posterior from a low-frequency zone on lateral Heschl's gyrus out to high-frequency zones in front of and behind it.
span.quote: Two mirror-symmetric frequency gradients were found extending along an anterior-posterior axis from a zone on the lateral aspect of Heschl's gyrus (HG), which responds preferentially to lower frequencies, toward zones posterior and anterior to HG that are sensitive to higher frequencies.

span.label: These principal gradients lie perpendicular to HG, overturning the prevailing assumption that they run parallel to it.
span.quote: The orientation of these two principal gradients is thus roughly perpendicular to HG, rather than parallel as previously assumed.

span.label: A third, smaller gradient was found on the lateral posterior superior temporal gyrus.
span.quote: A third, smaller gradient was observed in the lateral posterior aspect of the superior temporal gyrus.

span.label: The human maps are argued to be closely homologous to nonhuman primate auditory cortex, with the two main gradients corresponding to macaque A1 and R.
span.quote: Based on these similarities, it is likely that the two gradients observed in the current study encompass two separate regions of cortex homologous to macaque areas A1 and R.

span.label: Individual tonotopic maps were highly reproducible across separate scanning sessions.
span.quote: Overall, individual frequency selectivity maps were highly stable across sessions.

span.label: Regional differences in the preferred/non-preferred response ratio are driven by stronger responses to the preferred frequency, not by weaker responses to non-preferred ones.
span.quote: An inspection of the data without normalization ( Figure 8 ) suggests that these differences across brain areas are driven primarily by an increase in the response to the preferred frequency rather than a decrease in response to the non-preferred frequencies

span.label: two mirror-symmetric gradients run roughly perpendicular to HG, not parallel as previously assumed
span.quote: The orientation of these two principal gradients is thus roughly perpendicular to HG, rather than parallel as previously assumed.

span.label: a low-frequency zone on lateral HG is flanked anteriorly and posteriorly by high-frequency zones in every subject
span.quote: Also present in every subject are two high-frequency areas, located anterior and posterior to the low-frequency zone, that preferentially responded to frequencies at 6400 Hz.

span.label: a third, smaller gradient runs along lateral posterior STG, mainly in the left hemisphere
span.quote: This region appears to be part of a third, smaller gradient extending along the lateral posterior STG, mainly in the left hemisphere.

span.label: frequency-selective responses were confined to the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres
span.quote: In all subjects, areas with significant frequency selectivity were confined primarily to the superior temporal plane in both hemispheres

span.label: maps are highly reproducible across sessions within a subject
span.quote: Overall, individual frequency selectivity maps were highly stable across sessions.

span.label: the preferred/non-preferred difference is driven by a larger preferred response, not a smaller non-preferred one
span.quote: An inspection of the data without normalization ( Figure 8 ) suggests that these differences across brain areas are driven primarily by an increase in the response to the preferred frequency rather than a decrease in response to the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: no distinct frequency gradient in area CM, agreeing with macaque evidence for an overall high-frequency preference there
span.quote: In the posterior medial section of the map, which we label as area CM, there does not appear to be a distinct frequency gradient. This is in agreement with evidence from the macaque suggesting that the majority of neurons in this region respond preferentially to higher than average frequencies

span.label: prior imaging results and their interpretations varied considerably
span.quote: Results and interpretations from these studies have varied considerably.

span.label: four previous studies reached four different conclusions, one of them denying the gradients are gradients at all
span.quote: For example, one study reported a single high-to-low gradient extending from posterior medial to anterior lateral auditory areas, similar to earlier studies ( Langers, Backes, van Dijk 2007 ). A second study, however, described two mirror-symmetric frequency gradients (high-low-high) extending approximately along the axis of HG ( Formisano et al., 2003 ). In a third study, three consistent gradients were reported, none of which clearly follow the long axis of HG ( Talavage et al., 2004 ). Finally, the authors of a fourth study found differences in activation between anterior and posterior HG as well as medial and lateral differences, but concluded that the observed activation profile did not represent frequency gradients but instead different functional regions within the auditory cortex

span.label: tonotopy (cochleotopy)
span.quote: This organization, referred to as tonotopy or cochleotopy, mirrors the distribution of receptors in the cochlea, with a gradient extending between neurons that preferentially respond to high frequencies and those that respond best to low frequencies.

span.label: tuning bandwidth
span.quote: Differences in frequency selectivity (“tuning bandwidth”) were investigated by comparing the amplitude of the preferred (i.e., highest responding) frequency to the amplitudes of the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: frequency-selective response
span.quote: Voxels were identified as having a frequency-selective response if they showed significant differences in activation across the six frequencies as determined by an F test.

span.label: tonotopy
span.quote: This organization, referred to as tonotopy or cochleotopy, mirrors the distribution of receptors in the cochlea, with a gradient extending between neurons that preferentially respond to high frequencies and those that respond best to low frequencies.

span.label: frequency-selective response
span.quote: Voxels were identified as having a frequency-selective response if they showed significant differences in activation across the six frequencies as determined by an F test.

span.label: core/belt boundary
span.quote: with the boundary between core and belt defined by cytoarchitectonic and connectivity patterns rather than tonotopic gradients.

span.label: centre frequency of the multi-tone stimulus band
span.term: centre frequency of the multi-tone stimulus band
span.quote: Subjects were presented with stochastically alternating multi-tone sequences in six different frequency bands, centered at 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, and 6400 Hz.

span.label: frequency of maximum response at each cortical surface point
span.term: frequency of maximum response at each cortical surface point
span.quote: Points on the surface map that showed significant differences across frequency (i.e., tonotopy) were then labeled according to the frequency of maximum response.

span.label: mean BOLD signal per frequency condition
span.term: mean BOLD signal per frequency condition
span.quote: Estimates of the mean BOLD signal were calculated for each condition.

span.label: scanner drift (baseline, linear and quadratic nuisance terms)
span.term: scanner drift (baseline, linear and quadratic nuisance terms)
span.quote: Nuisance regressors included baseline, linear, and second-order polynomial terms for each run to reduce the effects of drift in the BOLD signal.

span.label: stimulus intensity
span.quote: The intensity of all tone sequences was normalized to A-weighted 76.3 dB.

span.label: centre frequency of the tone band
span.term: centre frequency of the tone band
span.quote: Subjects were presented with stochastically alternating multi-tone sequences in six different frequency bands, centered at 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, and 6400 Hz.

span.label: frequency of maximum response at a surface point
span.term: frequency of maximum response at a surface point
span.quote: Intermediate frequencies of best response at each point on the surface were determined by first selecting a subset of the frequencies that showed greater activation than the mean at that point. For the majority of surface points this consisted of one, two, or three adjacent frequencies. The activation levels for this set of frequencies were normalized to produce a weight vector, which was then multiplied by the corresponding log-transformed frequencies and summed. The resulting number was mapped to a log-scaled color map.

span.label: normalized response to non-preferred frequencies
span.quote: An inspection of the data without normalization ( Figure 8 ) suggests that these differences across brain areas are driven primarily by an increase in the response to the preferred frequency rather than a decrease in response to the non-preferred frequencies.

span.label: 8 — number of subjects scanned, with sex split and age range
span.quote: FMRI data were collected from 8 right-handed subjects (7 male, 1 female; ages 20-37 years).

span.label: 392 trials total — trials per scanning session, from 7 runs of 56 trials
span.quote: Each scanning session consisted of 7 functional runs, and each functional run consisted of 56 trials (392 trials total).

span.label: .834 (SD = 0.083) — mean correlation of a subject's tonotopy map between scanning sessions, i.e. test-retest stability
span.quote: The mean between-session correlation coefficient of the tonotopy maps is .834 (SD = 0.083).

span.label: 20 to 30 mm 3 — range of the per-subject cluster-size threshold used for multiple-comparison correction
span.quote: The resulting cluster thresholds varied between subjects, ranging from 20 to 30 mm 3

span.label: 76.3 dB — A-weighted intensity to which every tone sequence was normalised
span.quote: The intensity of all tone sequences was normalized to A-weighted 76.3 dB.

span.label: 9.6 seconds — trial length: an 8-second sound followed by a 1.6-second silent gap in which the scan was acquired
span.quote: A trial lasted 9.6 seconds and started with an 8-second tone sequence followed by a 1.6-second gap.

span.label: 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 6400 Hz — the six centre frequencies tested
span.quote: Subjects were presented with stochastically alternating multi-tone sequences in six different frequency bands, centered at 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, and 6400 Hz.

span.label: 8 right-handed subjects, 7 male and 1 female, ages 20-37 — the sample
span.quote: FMRI data were collected from 8 right-handed subjects (7 male, 1 female; ages 20-37 years).

span.label: .834, SD 0.083 — mean between-session correlation of the tonotopy maps
span.quote: The mean between-session correlation coefficient of the tonotopy maps is .834 (SD = 0.083).

span.label: better than 20 dB HL from 250 to 8000 Hz — audiometric inclusion criterion
span.quote: All subjects had normal hearing thresholds determined by a hearing test administered before scanning by a trained audiologist. Hearing thresholds were better than 20 dB HL in the range from 250 to 8000 Hz.

span.label: 20 to 30 mm3 — cluster threshold, which varied by subject because smoothness was estimated per subject
span.quote: The resulting cluster thresholds varied between subjects, ranging from 20 to 30 mm 3 .

span.label: 8 s stimulus then a 1.6 s scanning gap, 9.6 s per trial — the sparse-sampling timing
span.quote: A trial lasted 9.6 seconds and started with an 8-second tone sequence followed by a 1.6-second gap. MRI scanning was performed only during the 1.6-second gap to prevent interference from scanner noise during presentation of the stimulus.

span.label: 3000 Hz — Formisano's highest frequency, offered as the reason that study may have missed medial anterior high-frequency cortex
span.quote: The highest frequency used by Formisano et al. was 3000 Hz, whereas the current study included frequencies up to 6400 Hz, suggesting that some medial regions anterior to HG that are sensitive to higher frequencies might have been missed in the earlier study.

span.label: 3600 Hz, 4 Hz presentation rate — Woods' ceiling and rate, against 6400 Hz and 10 Hz here
span.quote: The highest frequency band tested by Woods et al. was 3600 Hz, compared to 6400 Hz in the current study. Compared to the stimuli in the current study, the pure tone sequences used by Woods et al. were presented at a slower frequency (4 Hz vs. 10 Hz) and had a narrower bandwidth.
